name: Bakry and Partitioning
description: Bakry faced a problem, but since he's lazy to solve it, he asks for your help. You are given a tree of $$$n$$$ nodes, the $$$i$$$-th node has value $$$a_i$$$ assigned to it for each $$$i$$$ from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$. As a reminder, a tree on $$$n$$$ nodes is a connected graph with $$$n-1$$$ edges. You want to delete at least $$$1$$$, but at most $$$k-1$$$ edges from the tree, so that the following condition would hold: For every connected component calculate the bitwise XOR of the values of the nodes in it. Then, these values have to be the same for all connected components. Is it possible to achieve this condition?
input_specification: Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases $$$t$$$ $$$(1 \leq t \leq 5 \cdot 10^4)$$$. Description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$k$$$ $$$(2 \leq k \leq n \leq 10^5)$$$. The second line of each test case contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_1, a_2, ..., a_n$$$ $$$(1 \leq a_i \leq 10^9)$$$. The $$$i$$$-th of the next $$$n-1$$$ lines contains two integers $$$u_i$$$ and $$$v_i$$$ ($$$1 \leq u_i, v_i \leq n$$$, $$$u_i\neq v_i$$$), which means that there's an edge between nodes $$$u_i$$$ and $$$v_i$$$. It is guaranteed that the given graph is a tree. It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ over all test cases doesn't exceed $$$2 \cdot 10^5$$$.
output_specification: For each test case, you should output a single string. If you can delete the edges according to the conditions written above, output "YES" (without quotes). Otherwise, output "NO" (without quotes). You can print each letter of "YES" and "NO" in any case (upper or lower).
approach_summary: Define tree DP state dp[u][state] computing optimal subproblem values for the subtree rooted at u. Aggregate transitions across children in post-order traversal in O(N × S) time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1592C — Bakry and Partitioning [463. DP on Trees and DAGs]
topic_editorial.summary: Tree Dynamic Programming with post-order traversal.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: A rooted tree has a clean hierarchical structure: removing the root decomposes the tree into independent disjoint subtrees. Therefore, the optimal solution for a subtree rooted at vertex $u$ depends purely on the solutions of its direct children $v \in \text{children}(u)$.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Root Selection & State Definition
Arbitrarily root the tree at node $1$. Define:
- $dp[u][0] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is excluded.
- $dp[u][1] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is included.

### Step 2: Post-Order DFS Traversal
We traverse the tree using depth-first search. A node $u$ computes its answers only after all its children $v \in \text{adj}[u]$ have computed theirs:
$$\text{dfs}(u, \text{parent})$$

### Step 3: Subtree Transition
For each child $v$ of $u$ ($v \ne \text{parent}$):
$$dp[u][0] = \sum_{v} \max(dp[v][0], dp[v][1])$$
$$dp[u][1] = \text{val}[u] + \sum_{v} dp[v][0]$$

### Step 4: Final Answer
At the root:
$$\text{Ans} = \max(dp[1][0], dp[1][1])$$
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Each node and edge in the tree is visited exactly once during the DFS traversal. All transitions at node $u$ run in time proportional to its degree. Summing across all vertices: $\sum \text{deg}(u) = 2(N-1) = \mathcal{O}(N)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Adjacency list storage takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, DP state arrays take $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, and the DFS call stack takes at most $\mathcal{O}(N)$ depth in the worst case.
